sections.title: What an interior designer invoice must show
sections.body: A standard template fails when applied to interior design because the trade blends services and physical goods. Your document needs distinct sections. Design fees must be clearly separated from furniture, fixtures, and equipment. If you are handling procurement, the invoice must clarify if you are acting as an agent buying on their account or reselling items at a margin. You also need clear line items for specification work, especially if the client buys the specified items from another vendor later. Use our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator to structure these details perfectly.
items: Separate line items for design fees and physical goods
Clear distinction between agency procurement and margin resale
Specific dates and locations for site visit charges
Detailed charges for specification and curation work

sections.title: How interior designer work is usually priced
sections.body: Designers rarely bill a single lump sum at the end of a project. Work is usually staged by design phase. You might charge a percentage upon signing, another after the concept presentation, and a final amount upon delivering the technical drawings. For physical goods, you might charge a procurement fee or apply a markup to trade prices. When clients want to handle their own purchasing, you must bill strictly for the specification list. Clear descriptions on every line prevent clients from confusing a design fee with the cost of a sofa.
items: Staged billing tied to specific design phases
Procurement fees calculated as a percentage of goods
Markup applied to trade prices for resold items
Flat fees for delivering a final specification list

sections.title: Getting paid: terms, deposits and chasing
sections.body: Cash flow is critical when ordering expensive custom furniture or fabrics. You must secure deposits before committing to vendors. Your invoice should clearly state the payment terms, such as requiring full payment for goods before the order is placed. Deducting initial design retainers from the final bill must be shown transparently so the client understands the remaining balance. If a client delays payment, sending a prompt payment reminder helps keep the project schedule on track without causing unnecessary friction.
items: Strict terms requiring payment before ordering custom goods
Clear deduction of initial retainers from final balances
Prompt payment reminders for overdue milestone invoices
Transparent bank details for large wire transfers

faqs.q: How do I invoice for procurement if I buy on the client's behalf?
faqs.a: If you buy on the client account, your invoice should only list your procurement fee, which is often a percentage of the total order value. You would provide the actual vendor receipts to the client separately for their records. Do not list the full price of the goods on your own invoice unless you are actively buying and reselling them at a margin.

faqs.q: Should I separate design fees from furniture costs?
faqs.a: Yes, you must always separate creative services from physical goods. Mixing them confuses clients and complicates your accounting. Create distinct sections on your invoice. List your design phases, site visits, and specification work in one area, and detail the furniture, fixtures, and equipment in another. This clarity helps clients understand exactly what they are funding.

faqs.q: How do I bill for a design specification list?
faqs.a: When a client pays you to select items but intends to buy them independently, you are billing for specification work. Create a line item for the curation and documentation of these choices. You can charge this as a flat fee or an hourly rate, ensuring you are compensated for your expertise regardless of where the items are purchased.

faqs.q: Can I show a deposit deduction on the final invoice?
faqs.a: Absolutely. When you reach the final design phase or final delivery, your invoice should list the total project cost, followed by a negative line item showing the initial deposit or retainer already paid. This clearly displays the remaining balance due, preventing any confusion over what the client has already contributed to the project.
